meta.home.title: EpiDetective — Open tools for reading health evidence
meta.home.desc: Free tools that let you explore what the World Health Organization has found about the causes of cancer. Built by a cancer epidemiologist at IARC/WHO.
meta.explorer.title: Cancer Evidence Explorer — EpiDetective
meta.explorer.desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is for each link. Built on the WHO's IARC Monographs.
home.eyebrow: Open tools for reading cancer evidence
home.h1: Translating epidemiological evidence for a healthier world
home.audience: For the curious public, patients, doctors, journalists, and the people who write health policy.
home.lede: EpiDetective builds free tools that let you explore published health research for yourself.
purpose.label: What this is
purpose.p1: Every tool here starts from research that is already published and already careful. The difficulty is that almost nobody outside the field can read it. Each tool rebuilds that research into something you can search, follow and question directly.
purpose.p2: The aim is to make findings usable while keeping the uncertainty that makes them trustworthy. Where the science is still unsure, the tool says so plainly.
inst.label: The tools
inst.h2: One is open now. More are being built.
inst.t1.name: Cancer Evidence Explorer
inst.t1.desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is behind each link. It is built on the IARC Monographs, the World Health Organization's review of what can cause cancer. Start from a cancer, start from an exposure, or open the whole map.
inst.t2.name: Occupational Exposure Atlas
inst.t2.desc: What people are exposed to at work, and which of those exposures carry an established cancer risk — drawing on job-exposure matrices from the SYNERGY and EPHOR cohorts.
inst.t3.name: Risk in Context
inst.t3.desc: A translator for the numbers that get misreported most, turning relative risks and hazard ratios into plain figures a person can weigh.
about.label: Who builds this
about.h2: Built by a cancer epidemiologist who works with this evidence every day.
about.p1: I am Wenxin Wan, a postdoctoral scientist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer in Lyon, the World Health Organization's cancer agency.
about.p2: I did my PhD at Utrecht University's Institute for Risk Assessment Sciences, studying how exposures at work and in the environment affect cancer risk. That work helped establish the causal role of benzene in lung cancer, and was covered by The New York Times.
about.p3: Day to day I work with large international cohort studies, following hundreds of thousands of people over many years to see which exposures are followed by disease. At IARC I lead the analysis for OPICO, which pools ten such cohorts across three continents to ask whether long-term opioid use carries a cancer risk, and I advise the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3) on how evidence about exposures at work can feed into lung cancer screening.
about.p4: I build these tools because the evidence I work with is public and carefully made, and still almost unreadable unless you already know the field. Closing that gap seemed worth the effort. Everything here is checkable, and the links go to the original sources.

exp.h1: Some exposures cause cancer. Some might. Telling them apart is the whole job.
exp.lede: Every mark behind this text is real: 186 exposures, 68 types of cancer, and the 466 links the World Health Organization's cancer agency has recorded between them.
exp.whatsin_h2: Every exposure the IARC has linked to a cancer, graded by how certain the evidence is.
exp.bar1_note: Studies in people agree closely enough to rule out chance, bias and other explanations. This is the strongest conclusion the IARC draws.
exp.bar2_note: There is a credible association, though chance or bias could still explain it. The question remains open, and more research may settle it either way.
exp.reads_h2: Three limits of this map, worth knowing before you read it.
exp.read1_h3: Something that can cause cancer may still have had nothing to do with yours.
exp.read1_p: A Group 1 classification means an exposure can cause cancer under some conditions. How much, for how long, at what age, and which genes you carry all stand between that finding and any one person.
exp.read2_h3: A missing link may only mean nobody has looked hard enough yet.
exp.read2_p: The map records what has been studied and reviewed. Many gaps come from limited research funding or short follow-up time, so an empty space here is weak evidence of safety.
exp.read3_h3: This map describes populations, and cannot judge any single case.
exp.read3_p: If you are living with a cancer diagnosis, the people treating you know things about your case that no population map contains. Bring your questions to them.
exp.cta_h2: Start from a cancer. Start from an exposure. Or open the whole map.
exp.cta_lede: Free, no account needed, available in ten languages. Drag, zoom, and focus on any part of the network.
exp.cta_source: Source: IARC Monographs, "Classifications by cancer site", Volumes 1–141a (last update 18 May 2026), adapted from Schubauer-Berigan et al., JNCI Monographs 2026. This tool identifies hazards across whole populations. For anything concerning your own health, speak to a doctor.
